b: Gemini audio generation API. You can use models such as gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts. POST /v1beta/models/{model}:generateContent

The native Gemini audio generation endpoint. Synthesize speech directly with models such as gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts, returning audio in PCM / WAV and other formats. Unlike the "Native OpenAI Format", this endpoint follows Google Gemini's v1beta protocol: you submit content to the generateContent endpoint and control the output modality and voice via generationConfig. Uter unifies access to the Gemini family of models — keys, quotas and billing all use the platform account system. Authenticate with a Bearer token. Authorization: Bearer <token> Content-Type: application/json 200 the request succeeded and JSON is returned. The generated audio is inlined in candidates[].content.parts[]. > Tip: the audio is inlined as base64 in inlineData.data; decode it according to inlineData.mimeType to play. Billing is based on input tokens — the synthesized audio is not billed as extra tokens.
Convert text to audio POST /v1/audio/speech Convert audio to text POST /v1/audio/transcriptions Translate audio into English text POST /v1/audio/translations

Two OpenAI-compatible billing endpoints let a client inspect the remaining quota and current-period usage of the credential in use. Both are available under /v1/dashboard/... and the legacy /dashboard/... prefix, and require a token (Authorization: Bearer sk-...). > The numeric USD fields follow the site's configured quota display type: with USD display they are converted from quota units at QuotaPerUnit; with CNY display they are converted to USD and multiplied by the exchange rate; with token display they carry the raw token count. Do not assume the suffix always means US dollars. GET /v1/dashboard/billing/subscription When token statistics are enabled for tokens, the figures reflect the token itself; otherwise they reflect the owning user's quota. An unlimited-quota token reports a large sentinel value (100000000). GET /v1/dashboard/billing/usage On an internal error this endpoint still returns HTTP 200 with an {"error": {...}} body (type utererror). Check for an error field rather than relying only on the status code.
Requests in the Anthropic Claude Messages API format. The anthropic-version header must be included in the request. POST /v1/messages

Gemini image, PDF, audio, and video recognition requests ⚠️ Note: Native Gemini format requests support passing media via inlineData (base64) or fileData.fileUri (a publicly accessible URL, including YouTube links). Whether a file URI uploaded through the Gemini File API is accessible depends on the permissions of the upstream channel key; publicly accessible URLs are recommended. When an OpenAI-format (chat/completions) request is converted to Gemini, media is downloaded and converted to inlineData (base64). POST /v1beta/models/{model}:generateContent Proxies Gemini API requests. Path format: /v1beta/models/{modelname}:{action} For example: - /v1beta/models/gemini-2.5-pro:generateContent - /v1beta/models/gemini-2.5-pro:streamGenerateContent?alt=sse POST /v1beta/models/{model}:generateContent

Uter's image endpoints are compatible with the OpenAI Images API. Only models returned by GET /v1/models can be used; supported sizes, quality levels and model-specific parameters differ, and out-of-range values are rejected with 400. POST /v1/images/generations POST /v1/images/edits This endpoint accepts both multipart/form-data (file uploads) and application/json (image passed as a URL or base64 string). Use the content type that matches your client. Same structure as "Generate an image"; the fields inside data follow responseformat.
Bailian qwen-image series image generation POST /v1/images/generations Bailian qwen-image series image editing POST /v1/images/edits

Uter exposes four model lookup endpoints: The list is filtered by the token's group, its model allowlist and model billing configuration. Trust the returned list and do not hardcode model names. GET /v1/models selects the response format from the request headers: - x-api-key and anthropic-version headers → Anthropic format - x-goog-api-key header or key query parameter → Gemini format - Otherwise → OpenAI format See "Native OpenAI Format" and "Native Gemini Format" for the fields and example responses of each format.

Returns the available models in the Gemini API format. Authentication: use the ?key=sk-... query parameter or the x-goog-api-key header. The list is filtered by the token's group and model allowlist. GET /v1beta/models

GET /v1/models Returns the models the current token can call. The list is filtered by the token's group, the token's model allowlist and model billing configuration, so different tokens may see different lists. The response format is selected from the request headers: - x-api-key and anthropic-version headers → Anthropic format - x-goog-api-key header or key query parameter → Gemini format - Otherwise → OpenAI format GET /v1/models/{model} Returns the model object (fields as above) when it exists. When it does not, the response is still 200, with an error body instead: Check for an error field in the body rather than relying on the HTTP status alone.
Check whether text content violates the usage policy POST /v1/moderations

Establish a WebSocket connection for real-time conversations. Note: This is a WebSocket endpoint and must be connected using the WebSocket protocol. Connection URL example: wss://uter.ai/v1/realtime?model=gpt-4o-realtime Authentication: send Authorization: Bearer sk-... in the handshake headers. Browser clients that cannot set headers can use the Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: openai-insecure-api-key.sk-... subprotocol instead. GET /v1/realtime
Re-rank a list of documents by relevance to a query POST /v1/rerank

The OpenAI Responses API supports multi-turn conversations, tool calls, reasoning and server-side response state. Uter exposes create, retrieve, WebSocket streaming and compaction endpoints. A single token reaches any channel that serves the openai-response endpoint family (for example Uter Route / Uter API / Codex and OpenAI-compatible channels). Model IDs come from GET /v1/models. Requests for models that do not support this endpoint family are rejected; the token's group and model allowlist still apply. > Note: POST /v1/responses and GET /v1/responses/{responseid} are host-protocol endpoints. For a model claimed by a task plugin the plugin handles the call; otherwise the request falls back to the built-in Responses relay. POST /v1/responses GET /v1/responses/{responseid} Returns a previously stored response by ID. The response body uses the same fields as create. An unknown ID returns an OpenAI-format error. GET /v1/responses A WebSocket endpoint for streaming responses. Channel selection happens after the first response.create event, and each event runs through the ordinary request limiter. Clients that cannot set handshake headers may authenticate with the Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: openai-insecure-api-key.<key> subprotocol, in addition to Authorization: Bearer. Connection URL: wss://uter.ai/v1/responses POST /v1/responses/compact Compacts the conversation state of a response to reduce the token count of a continued session. The response uses the same object shape as create, with the compacted conversation in output.

Uter exposes two families of search/tool relay endpoints. The raw request body is forwarded to the upstream and the upstream response is returned unchanged. Calls are billed by request at the routing model's price (no token count). These endpoints are available only on channels that support them; a channel that does not returns an error and the request may be retried on another eligible channel. POST /v1/alpha/search Standalone web search used by Codex-style clients. Supported on Uter Route / Uter API / Sub2API / NewAPI / Codex / Advanced Custom channels and provider-plugin channels. Additional provider-specific fields are passed through unchanged. The response body is the upstream response, returned as-is. POST /v1/tools/search POST /v1/tools/fetch Web search and page fetch tools used by DeepSeek-style clients. Supported on DeepSeek, Uter Route / Uter API, Sub2API, NewAPI and Advanced Custom channels, plus provider-plugin channels. The model names deepseek-search and deepseek-fetch select the corresponding endpoint family. All other fields are provider-specific and passed through unchanged. The response body is the upstream response, returned as-is.

The generic task API is the provider-agnostic surface for asynchronous work (image and video generation, and other task plugins). It is the format behind /v1/video/generations and is also available directly under /v1/tasks/. Task IDs are shared across both entry points. All endpoints require a token (Authorization: Bearer sk-...). Artifact content download additionally accepts scoped artifact-access authorization. POST /v1/tasks/{key} The key path segment is the task-plugin key. The body is provider-specific; a model field selects the channel and billing, and provider options are passed through. The response carries a task ID (taskid / id) and an initial status (usually queued). GET /v1/tasks/{key} Here key is the task ID returned at submission. Returns the unified task envelope: A missing task, or one owned by another user, returns 400 with code: tasknotexist. GET /v1/tasks/{key}/artifacts Returns the artifacts produced by a completed task (for example generated files). GET /v1/tasks/{key}/artifacts/{artifactkey}/content HEAD /v1/tasks/{key}/artifacts/{artifactkey}/content Streams the artifact file. HEAD returns the same headers without a body. This endpoint accepts either a regular token or a scoped artifact-access credential.

This endpoint is not implemented. POST /v1/fine-tunes/{finetuneid}/cancel This endpoint is not implemented. POST /v1/fine-tunes This endpoint is not implemented. GET /v1/fine-tunes/{finetuneid}/events This endpoint is not implemented. GET /v1/fine-tunes This endpoint is not implemented. GET /v1/fine-tunes/{finetuneid}

Video generation is asynchronous: submit a task, poll its status, then fetch the result. Uter exposes two entry points: - Generic task format: /v1/video/generations returns a taskid; provider-specific options go in metadata. - OpenAI video format: /v1/videos accepts OpenAI Videos fields. For a model bound to an openaivideo task plugin, both request and response follow the OpenAI Videos API and the official SDK works unchanged. For models not claimed by such a plugin, the request falls back to the generic task relay and the response uses the task envelope below (taskid, status: queued) instead of an OpenAI video object. Request fields differ per provider; read the provider-specific pages below as well. POST /v1/video/generations Some providers render the response directly from a task plugin; in that case the fields follow the provider page. GET /v1/video/generations/{taskid} Returns Uter's unified task envelope (code is success on success): A missing task, or one owned by another user, returns 400 (tasknotexist). POST /v1/videos accepts application/json and multipart/form-data with the OpenAI Videos fields: model, prompt, seconds, size, inputreference, and so on. The response is an OpenAI video object: Companion endpoints: Note the status-code difference: GET /v1/videos/{id}/content returns 404 for an unknown task, while the generic task query GET /v1/video/generations/{taskid} returns 400 tasknotexist. status values: queued, inprogress, completed, failed.

HappyHorse video generation: call the full HappyHorse 1.0 model family through an asynchronous task API, supporting text-to-video, image-to-video, reference-to-video and video editing. All four models share a single endpoint, /v1/video/generations, and are distinguished only by the model field; the response shape is identical. Submit a video generation task and receive a task ID; poll the status endpoint for the result. POST /v1/video/generations > id / taskid is generated by Uter and is not the upstream DashScope taskid. Always use the value returned here. GET /v1/video/generations/{taskid} The response uses Uter's unified {code, message, data} envelope. Pass the following through the request body's metadata object; Uter forwards them to upstream DashScope. > i2v does not support ratio; the aspect ratio follows the input first-frame image. r2v and video-edit pass media via the metadata.input.media array: For r2v, reference images by array order in the prompt using [Image 1], [Image 2]. > video-edit output length: input ≤ 15s yields the same length; input > 15s is truncated to the first 15s. Besides /v1/video/generations, an OpenAI-style /v1/videos endpoint is available; the two are fully equivalent (same backend task). - Submit: POST /v1/videos (identical body fields) - Query: GET /v1/videos/{taskid} (returns the flat OpenAI format) Common FAILURE causes: content moderation rejection (adjust the prompt), missing inputreference for i2v, zero reference images for r2v, missing video for video-edit, unreachable media URL, or media that violates the constraints above.

Video generation API in the official Jimeng API format. The operation type can be specified with the Action parameter: - CVSync2AsyncSubmitTask: Submit a video generation task - CVSync2AsyncGetResult: Get the task result Action and Version must be specified in the query parameters. POST /jimeng/

Generate videos from an image with the Kling model. The image parameter accepts either an image URL or Base64-encoded image data. POST /kling/v1/videos/image2video Generate videos from a text description with the Kling model. Supported models: kling-v1, kling-v1-5, etc. POST /kling/v1/videos/text2video Query the status and result of a Kling image-to-video task. GET /kling/v1/videos/image2video/{taskid} Query the status and result of a Kling text-to-video task. GET /kling/v1/videos/text2video/{taskid}

MiniMax H3 (MiniMax-H3) video generation: call MiniMax H3 through an asynchronous task API, supporting text-to-video, image-to-video and reference-to-video, billed precisely against upstream usage. There is a single model name, MiniMax-H3. The generation mode is decided automatically by which media inputs the request carries: In every mode, prompt is always required. POST /v1/video/generations Used for reference-to-video (r2v) to specify each reference asset's role precisely: When structured media is omitted, Uter infers assets from images / inputreference by extension and order: video → reference video, audio → reference audio, 1st image → first frame, 2nd image → last frame. Use media[] when you need precise role control. > Reference audio (referenceaudio) is currently limited by upstream support: in testing the upstream returns task failure (Uter refunds in full automatically). Text-to-video, image-to-video (first frame / first+last frame) and reference image/video generation all work normally. > id / taskid is generated by Uter and is not the upstream MiniMax taskid. GET /v1/video/generations/{taskid} The response uses Uter's unified {code, message, data} envelope. MiniMax H3 bills against the actual upstream usage: Key points: - Input reference video is billed too: for r2v, a reference video's billable duration is counted at the output resolution's price. - Reference images are billed separately: $0.04 per billable reference image. - Pre-charged on submit, settled on completion: a provisional charge is taken at submit time, then Uter recomputes precisely from the upstream usage on success, refunding or charging the difference. Reference-to-video using the top-level media[] array:

PixVerse video generation through the OpenAI-compatible /v1/videos endpoint, supporting text-to-video and image-to-video. > Availability: PixVerse is not a built-in provider channel. These model IDs are available only if your administrator has configured a custom channel (Advanced Custom / Uter Route) that serves them. Check GET /v1/models for the exact IDs your token can call; if no PixVerse/ model is listed, this format is unavailable on your account. When a PixVerse channel is configured, use the form PixVerse/<version> in the model field, e.g. PixVerse/v5.6. The tiers below describe the PixVerse upstream convention; the models actually exposed depend on the channel configuration. > The PixVerse/ prefix is case-sensitive; use PixVerse/v5.6 exactly. The version part (v5.6, c1) is normalised case-insensitively. POST /v1/videos > id / taskid is generated by Uter and is not the upstream PixVerse videoid. Always use the value returned here. GET /v1/videos/{taskid} GET /v1/videos/{taskid}/content Returns the raw video stream (Content-Type: video/mp4). Uter proxies PixVerse's temporary URL, avoiding exposure of the upstream address and the expiry problem. > Strongly recommended: download via the /content proxy rather than accessing metadata.url directly. The latter is PixVerse's temporary link (usually valid for a few hours), whereas the proxy never expires as long as the task record exists. All PixVerse-specific fields are passed through the request body's metadata object. > motionmode: fast is strictly limited to V4.5 / V4 / V3.5, 5-second duration and 360p/540p/720p. Other combinations (e.g. 1080p + fast or 8s + fast) return 400 and are not charged. > V5 / V4.5 / V4 / V3.5 do not support audio; passing generateaudioswitch: true returns 400. PixVerse image-to-video requires uploading the image upstream to obtain an imgid. Uter wraps the upload flow automatically: pass image: "https://..." or image: "data:image/png;base64,..." in the body and Uter uploads it to PixVerse, retrieves the imgid and forwards it. If you already have an imgid (advanced case), pass it directly:

Seedance video generation (Dreamina): call the Dreamina Seedance 2.0 model family through an asynchronous task API, supporting text-to-video, image-to-video and video continuation / editing. Both models support video as input (continuation / editing) by passing videourl inside metadata.content. POST /v1/video/generations > id / taskid is generated by Uter and is not the upstream task id. GET /v1/video/generations/{taskid} The response is a {code, message, data} envelope; on success code is "success" and data is the task detail object. GET /v1/videos/{taskid}/content Returns the raw video stream (Content-Type: video/mp4). Uter proxies the upstream URL. > Strongly recommended: download via the /content proxy rather than accessing resulturl directly, which is an upstream temporary link with a limited lifetime. All Seedance-specific fields are passed through the request body's metadata object and forwarded upstream. Besides the top-level image / images fields, you can pass a multimodal input array in metadata.content, mixing images and videos: Suggested handling: adjust the prompt on moderation failures; switch to base64 when URLs are unreachable; retry later or switch to dreamina-seedance-2-0-fast on upstream timeouts.

OpenAI-compatible video generation API. Reference: https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/videos/create POST /v1/videos OpenAI-compatible video task status query API. Returns detailed status information for a video task. GET /v1/videos/{taskid} Generate again from an existing video (remix); the new task reuses the original video's channel and model. POST /v1/videos/{videoid}/remix Returns a new OpenAI video object with the same fields as "Create Video". A missing video, or one owned by another user, returns 400. Get the video file content of a completed video task. This endpoint proxies and returns the video file stream. GET /v1/videos/{taskid}/content

Google Veo 3.1 video generation: call the full Veo 3.1 model family through an asynchronous task API, supporting text-to-video and image-to-video with optional synchronised audio (up to 4K output). All three models share a single endpoint and are distinguished only by the model field. Every model supports text-to-video and image-to-video, with optional audio generation. POST /v1/video/generations > Top-level snakecase fields such as generateaudio / negativeprompt / aspectratio are automatically mapped to upstream camelCase parameters. You may also place them inside metadata (snakecase or camelCase), which is equivalent to the top level. > > generateaudio: true significantly increases cost (roughly 2×). As the billing default is true, set generateaudio: false explicitly when audio is not needed. GET /v1/video/generations/{taskid} The response uses Uter's unified {code, message, data} envelope. image / images[0] accept the following three formats; Uter detects and converts them to the inline base64 that Veo expects: Limits: decoded size ≤ 20 MB; URL download timeout 30 seconds; parse failures (unreachable URL / too large / invalid base64) return 400 parse images[0] failed: ... with no charge. Native gs:// GCS URIs are not supported; use https://storage.googleapis.com/... instead. metadata is a Veo-native parameter container for advanced options not present in the OpenAI style. All top-level fields may also be placed inside metadata (snakecase or camelCase). > Precedence: camelCase already in metadata > snakecase in metadata > top-level fields. Besides /v1/video/generations, an OpenAI-style /v1/videos endpoint is available; the two are fully equivalent. - Submit: POST /v1/videos (identical body fields) - Query: GET /v1/videos/{taskid} (returns the flat OpenAI format) > The OpenAI-compatible query response does not include the video URL. To obtain the download address, use /v1/video/generations/{taskid} and read data.url. On failed, Uter refunds automatically. First+last-frame interpolation (Veo 3.1 exclusive): - referenceimages cannot be combined with image / images / lastframeimage, otherwise 400 referenceimages is mutually exclusive ... is returned. - referenceimages accepts at most 3 entries; more returns 400 referenceimages supports at most 3 entries. - referenceimages is only supported for duration=8. Common failed causes: content safety rejection (adjust

Wan 2.7 video generation: call the full Wan 2.7 model family through an asynchronous task API, supporting text-to-video, image-to-video, reference-to-video and video editing, with 1080P output, videos up to 15 seconds, multi-shot narrative and native audio synchronisation. All four models share a single endpoint, /v1/video/generations, and are distinguished only by the model field; the response shape is identical. POST /v1/video/generations > The images field is in a release transition period: before the release, pass media via the metadata.input.media array; after it, the system infers media types from URL extensions and images can be used directly. > id / taskid is generated by Uter and is not the upstream DashScope taskid. Always use the value returned here. GET /v1/video/generations/{taskid} The response uses Uter's unified {code, message, data} envelope. Pass the following through the request body's metadata object; Uter forwards them to upstream DashScope. > i2v does not support ratio; the aspect ratio follows the input first-frame image. For r2v and videoedit, pass media through the metadata.input.media array: For r2v, reference images by array order in the prompt using [Image 1], [Image 2]. Besides /v1/video/generations, an OpenAI-style /v1/videos endpoint is available; the two are fully equivalent. - Submit: POST /v1/videos (identical body fields) - Query: GET /v1/videos/{taskid} (returns the flat OpenAI format) Wan 2.7 bills by seconds × resolution factor: On FAILURE, Uter refunds automatically. For videoedit, pass media via the images array: the 1st MP4/MOV is the video to edit and the remaining PNG/JPG/WEBP entries are reference images; duration is not required (it follows the input video). Common FAILURE causes: DataInspectionFailed (upstream safety rejection — adjust the prompt or assets), missing inputreference for i2v, zero reference images for r2v, images[0] not being MP4/MOV for videoedit, unreachable media URL, or media that violates the constraints above.

Claude format (/v1/messages) also accepts an x-api-key header; Gemini format (/v1beta/models/...) accepts an x-goog-api-key header or a ?key= query parameter. WebSocket endpoints additionally accept the Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: openai-insecure-api-key.<key> subprotocol for browser clients that cannot set headers. The error envelope depends on the endpoint family. Always branch on the body, not only the HTTP status: A few endpoints are exceptions: GET /v1/models/{model} returns 200 with an OpenAI error body for an unknown model, and GET /v1/videos/{id}/content returns 404 for a missing task while the generic task query returns 400 tasknotexist. A single token reaches every upstream provider aggregated by the platform. Endpoints are grouped below by protocol family; see the linked page for request/response fields. Which models a token can call is decided by its group, the token's model allowlist and the model's billing configuration. Always use the model names returned by GET /v1/models; do not guess model IDs. - When a request is accepted, quota is pre-deducted from the model price and the estimated usage, then settled against the actual usage. Failed requests and tasks that produced no output are refunded. - Insufficient quota returns 403; rate limiting or saturated upstream concurrency returns 429; an unknown model or no channel available in the current group returns 503. - Image generation count n is capped at 128. Video duration, resolution and batch size follow the selected model's limits; out-of-range requests are rejected before acceptance. /v1/files, /v1/fine-tunes, /v1/images/variations and DELETE /v1/models/{model} currently return 501. Gemini :countTokens returns 404. Do not call them in production. Fine-tuning is documented separately on the [fine-tuning page](./ai-model-unimplemented-fine-tuning).

b: Before wiring a model into Uter, verify it step by step — can it connect, can it answer, is it stable, is it billed correctly — so problems surface before production. Start with the Playground in the console, then re-check over the API. That split quickly separates “the model is unavailable” from “my request is wrong”. Confirm you have the items below. Missing any one of them makes step 1 fail. - Group: determines billing ratio and the routable model set. A key bills and routes according to its group. - Channel: the upstream provider that actually serves a model (e.g. Uter channel, aggregate channel, shared channel). One model can be served by several enabled channels, or by a single one. The same model can therefore differ in availability and price across groups and over time. “No available channel” means no enabled channel currently serves that model for your group — not that your request is malformed. An API key is a password: use it only server-side or in a secret manager. Never send it to a browser, never log it in plaintext, never commit it. API keys have four states: Enabled, Disabled, Expired, Exhausted. Creating or editing a key can also apply: - Group: determines the billing ratio and routable models; an “auto group order” and cross-group retry can be configured as well. - Expiry: “Never expires” by default; after expiry calls return 401. - Quota cap: entered in the configured site currency (USD by default), or “Unlimited”. When used up the key becomes Exhausted. - Model limits: allow only selected models. With no model selected the key cannot call anything. - IP allowlist: supports CIDR (e.g. 203.0.113.0/24); other sources are rejected. - Allow querying user quota: whether this key may call /v1/dashboard/billing/. - Quantity: several keys can be generated at once; keep one for testing. For a test key, allow only the model under test and turn off cross-group retry. Otherwise requests may route to unexpected channels and invalidate your connectivity or billing conclusions. Chat → Playground exercises the same model path as the API. 1. Open the model selector: pick a channel in the left pane and one of its models in the right pane. The first channel in the list is selected by default. 2. Send a message and watch the reply (streamed by default). 3. Open Parameter settings and enable what you need: temperature, topp, maxtokens, frequencypenalty, presen

Audit logs capture security-relevant events such as logins, settings changes and administrative actions. They are read-only and independent of usage logs. Columns include Time, Username, Event, IP, Client, Method, Route, HTTP status, Result and Details. Every sign-in and configuration change leaves an entry. Narrow the list with Date Range, Result and Category filters, then press Search. This is the fastest way to investigate a suspicious login. Press Details on a row to see the full payload: actor, action, route, status and the request context recorded at the time. Audit records are retained for security review and cannot be edited from the console.

If the button is missing, that provider has been disabled by the administrator. With the agreement accepted, select Continue with Discord (shown selected below) and approve the authorization on Discord. You are redirected back to the console on success. OAuth sign-in uses your GitHub or Discord identity — you can bind or unbind these providers later under Security & Access. The agreement checkbox must be ticked before any sign-in method works. Session cookies are HttpOnly and rotated on login.

Daily Check-in grants a small random quota reward once per day. It is a simple way to earn a little extra credit for regular use. Press Check in now to receive today’s reward. Each check-in gives a random amount of quota; the page shows your total check-ins and cumulative reward. The monthly calendar marks the days you have already checked in. Use Previous month and Next month to review earlier activity — a day can only be claimed once. Missing a day breaks the run, so check in regularly to build up the habit.

The data dashboard turns your request history into charts, helping you see which models you use, how costs trend, and where traffic flows. Model Call Analytics aggregates requests by model. Use the tabs to switch views and the Filter control to narrow by model, token or time range. The Call Trend, Call Count Distribution and Call Count Ranking cards visualise volume over time. Toggle between Bar Chart and Area Chart, and open Preferences to customise the metrics shown. The Flow tab presents traffic as a funnel from request to completion. It is useful for spotting where requests are dropped or retried. Combine a time filter with a single model to isolate the cost of one workload.

Overview is the landing page after sign-in. It summarises your balance and usage, exposes the API connection details, and answers common onboarding questions. On your first visit, the setup guide is expanded at the top of the page, bringing everything you need before going live into one place. It lists three steps in order: Create an API Key (generate a credential for your app or service), Add credits (keep a healthy balance before production traffic), and Send a request (verify routing with the Playground or your own client). Completed steps show a check mark. On the right, the guide shows a First API request example you can copy in one click, plus three live readiness indicators: Route active, Auth configured, and Model selected. The Recommended actions column on the far right links to API Keys, Usage Logs, and Pricing. Once you are connected, click Hide setup guide to collapse it. The top cards show your current balance, today’s requests and recent consumption. These numbers come from the same quota ledger that billing uses, so they reflect real deductions. The API Info card lists your Base URL and shows a Copy URL button. Point your OpenAI-compatible client at this address, then use a key from API Keys to authenticate. The FAQ accordion covers what Uter is, registration, Base URL, supported models, pricing, top-ups, error codes (401 / 429 / timeout), data safety, balance queries and support. Click any question to expand its answer. The Uptime panel reports service availability over time. A dip here usually corresponds to a maintenance window or an upstream provider incident. Use the Setup guide on this page if this is your first time connecting a client.

The Playground lets you try any available model directly in the browser, with no API key or code. It is the fastest way to compare answers and tune parameters before integrating. The main chat area shows the conversation as a transcript. Type a message and press Send to call the selected model; replies stream in token by token. Clear chat history resets the conversation. The Attach button adds files for models that accept them, and Search enables web lookup where supported. Quick prompts such as Analyze data, Summarize text, Code and Get advice fill the input with a ready-made instruction. They are useful starting points when you want to probe a model’s strengths quickly. The model selector at the bottom switches between the models you are entitled to use. Each entry shows the model id and its provider tag, so you can test exactly the same model your API calls will hit. Open Parameters to adjust sampling controls such as temperature and top-p. Lower values make answers more deterministic; higher values increase variety. Changes apply to the next message only. Playground calls count against your quota just like API requests, so it is a realistic preview of production cost.

Pricing is the live catalog of models and their prices. It is the authoritative source for what a request costs before you send it. Each card shows the model name, provider and price tiers. Use Filter to narrow by provider or capability, and switch between Card view and Table view. The Standard badge indicates the pricing mode. Prices are shown per million tokens (/1M) or per thousand (/1K) depending on the model, with separate input and output rates. Toggle the unit to compare models on the same basis. Open Details on a model to see its full rate card, supported capabilities and context limits. Use Copy model name to paste the exact id into your application. Prices reflect the current catalog and may differ from what was charged for older requests — check Usage Logs for historical charges.

Settings controls how the console notifies you and presents itself. These preferences are per-user and do not affect other members. Under Notification Method, enable the channels you want — Email, Webhook, Bark or Gotify — and configure their endpoints. Press Save Settings to apply. Notifications to receive lets you choose which events trigger a message, such as low balance, failed login or completed task, so you only hear about what matters. In Preferences, set the Interface Language. The guide serves the same chapter URL in every language, so switching language keeps you on the same page. Sidebar Personal Settings controls which items appear in the Chat Area, Console Area and Personal Center Area. Hide sections you never use with Reset to Default to restore the standard layout. Webhook notifications require a reachable URL; test the endpoint before relying on it.

Rankings show which models are popular across the platform, along with market share and momentum. Use the period tabs to change the time window. The LLM Leaderboard ranks models by usage in the selected period. Use Today / Week / Month / Year to switch the window and see how preferences shift. Market Share groups usage by model author, showing the relative footprint of each provider on the platform. Trending up and Trending down highlight the fastest-growing and fastest-declining models, useful for spotting new releases gaining traction. Rankings aggregate anonymised usage — they reveal no individual account data.

Redemption codes add quota to your account. They are commonly distributed as promotions, referrals or compensation. Enter the code in the Redemption Code field and press Redeem. On success the code’s quota is credited to your balance immediately and the code is consumed. The credited amount is shown in the account balance card. Codes are single-use; an already-redeemed or expired code returns an error and does not change your balance. Never share a valid code publicly — the first person to redeem it consumes it.

The Referral Program rewards you when new users join through your link. Accumulated rewards can be moved into your spendable balance. Copy the referral link and share it. When a new user signs up through it and meets the site’s qualifying rules, a reward is credited to your referral earnings. Use Transfer to Balance to move accumulated referral earnings into your main balance so they can be spent on API calls. The dialog confirms the amount before it is moved. Referral rewards and top-up quota are tracked separately so you can see what each channel earns.

Security & Access centralises password, two-factor authentication, login sessions and API access tokens. Review it periodically to keep your account safe. Change Password rotates your login password. Account Bindings shows whether Email, GitHub and Discord are linked, with a Bind action for each unconnected provider. Enable Two-Step Verification to add TOTP-based 2FA; keep the backup codes somewhere safe. You can also toggle Record IP Address under Privacy and press Save Settings. Access records shows recent security events. Login sessions lists active devices — use Sign out other sessions to revoke them. Access tokens are for calling the dashboard API from scripts; create one with Create access token and Revoke it when no longer needed. The Delete Account action is permanent and removes all data. It cannot be undone.

Task logs track asynchronous jobs such as image generation, music creation and other model-driven tasks that complete after submission. The table shows Submit Time, Task ID, Duration, Status, Progress, Artifacts and Details. Statuses include queued, processing, succeeded and failed. Click View details to inspect the task payload, progress history and generated artifacts, including retry information when a task fails. Switch to the Drawing Logs tab for image-specific jobs, with quick access to generated images and their parameters. Tasks are billed when they complete; a failed task that consumed upstream resources still appears here.

Usage logs record every model request with its token usage and cost. Use them to reconcile billing and diagnose failed calls. Each row shows Time, Token, Model, Stream, Tokens, Cost, Timing and a Details action. The page is paginated and reflects the selected date range. Use the date-range picker and the All Types dropdown to narrow by time and request type, then press Search. Reset clears all filters. Click View on a row to open the detail dialog. It shows the request and response, token breakdown, the exact charge, and timing — this is the authoritative source for a disputed charge. Export downloads the filtered results as a file for offline analysis or accounting. Failed requests that consume upstream tokens are still logged with their cost.

The Wallet holds your credit balance and is the entry point for top-ups and subscriptions. Every request deducts from it; when it is empty, calls fail fast with an insufficient-balance error. The Add Funds card offers preset amounts with their payment prices, plus a custom-amount field bounded by a minimum. Choose a Payment Method — the list is driven by server configuration and can include Alipay, WeChat, Stripe and others. The Amount to pay: line converts quota into the payment currency at the live exchange rate. Order History lists every top-up attempt, including expired ones, with its status (Success / Pending / Expired) and a searchable trade number. Quote the trade number in any support request. The Subscription Plans card shows each plan’s quota, validity period, quota-reset schedule and purchase limit; a Recommended tag marks the admin’s pick. Subscribe Now starts the payment flow, and subscribed plans appear with an upgrade option where applicable. Use a real payment method for live top-ups; the demo figures shown here are for illustration only.
